intensifying or emphasizing particle, indeed (dated: Pyramid Texts to New Kingdom and Greco-Roman Period)
[in clauses with a verbal predicate in the perfect] marks a statement as hypothetical or contrafactual
definitions.usage_notes:
This particle is enclitic; it follows the word which it is intensifying or marking as contrafactual. It can also apply its effect to whole phrases. Often the exact nuance imparted by this particle is unclear.

Frequently this particle is found following (and thus adding emphasis to) jsṯ, ḥwj, m.k, or ḥꜣ, and in the Pyramid Texts it is also found in nominal sentences preceding pw. In Neo-Middle Egyptian it precedes rather than follows jsṯ and js but is often found following jw.

etymologies.etymology_text:
===Etymology 3===
According to the Rösslerian school of Egyptian comparison, from earlier {{m|egy|*lꜥꜥ}}, from {{inh|egy|afa-pro|*laɣ- |*laɣ- (?)|to speak}}; compare {{cog|sem-pro|*lɣz}}, {{cog|ar|لَغَزَ|tr=|t=to speak enigmatically, to use puzzling or riddle-like language}}, {{cog|he|לעז||to speak a foreign language}}.<ref>{{R:egy:Loprieno|31}}</ref>

definitions: [intransitive, Late Egyptian] to speak a foreign language, to gibber
[Late Egyptian] speaker of a foreign language, generally a foreigner or interpreter

, Papyrus Harris I, plate 15a, lines 7–10:Erichsen, Wolja (1933) Papyrus Harris I: Hieroglyphische Transkription, Brussels, p.18Birch, Samuel (1876) Facsimile of an Egyptian Hieratic papyrus of the reign of Ramses III, now in the British Museum, London, p.9 and Plate 15a
definitions.usage_notes: There seems to be some confusion over the determinative used in this word; Lesko renders it W23, while Erman and Grapow render it W6, but in the slips used for compiling their dictionary it is rendered identically to W24. The original word (and so the determinative) is attested only in hieratic, where the sign most closely resembles other hieratic writings of W24.See, for instance, the signs in Möller, Georg (1909​–1936) Hieratische Paläographie, Leipzig, vol. 1, pp. 47–48.

etymologies.etymology_text:
==Egyptian==

===Etymology===
Most likely from the infinitive of {{m|egy|ꜣwj-jb||to be happy}}; however, some instead suggest a derivation directly from {{af|egy|ꜣwt|t1=length|jb|t2=heart}} in a direct genitive construction. The former would imply the noun is masculine; the latter, feminine. It is attested a few times modified by (apparently masculine) {{m|egy|nb}}, suggesting that the former is the case, but the omission of feminine adjective endings is also not unusual.

===Pronunciation===
{{egy-IPA-E}}

definitions: a pectoral amulet in the form of the hieroglyphs  ligatured, presumably intended to bring the wearer happiness (dated: Greco-Roman Period)
definitions.usage_notes: These amulets are attested long before the word for them appears in the textual record; older instances of the word have apparently not survived.

definitions: realgar (red arsenic sulfide) (dated: since the New Kingdom)
definitions.usage_notes: Before the Late Period this term is found almost exclusively in medical texts (Papyrus Chester Beatty V and Papyrus Ebers).

==Egyptian==

===Etymology===
Gardiner hypothesizes a relation with {{m|egy|ꜣḫfḫf||to blaze (of the eyes)}}, for which compare also {{m|egy|ḫfꜣj||to illuminate}}. Federn, following a different interpretation of the word, contrarily proposes a connection with {{m|egy|ḫfꜣt||food}}, {{m|egy|ḫfꜣ||to fill with, to be swelled with}}, and {{m|egy|ḫfḫf}}.

===Pronunciation===
{{egy-IPA-E}}

==Egyptian==

===Etymology===
Perhaps a {{rdp|egy|ꜣḫf||burning appetite{{sup|?}}|nocap=1}}. Compare also {{m|egy|ḫfꜣj||to illuminate}}.

===Pronunciation===
{{egy-IPA-E}}

==Egyptian==
{{wikipedia|Aker (god)}}

===Etymology===
Cognate with {{cog|ber-pro|*a-kal||earth}} (whence {{cog|tzm|ⴰⵛⴰⵍ}}, {{cog|tmh|ăkall}}, and {{cog|rif|šar}}).

{{false cognate|sux|𒀳|t=farmer|tr=engar}}, and therefore unrelated to any of its descendants such as {{ncog|akk|ikkarum|alt=𒅅𒅗𒀸|tr=ikkarum}}, {{ncog|he|אִיכָּר|tr=ʔikkā́r}}, {{ncog|ar|أَكَّار}}, etc.

===Pronunciation===
{{egy-IPA-E}}

definitions: Aker, the Egyptian god of the earth and the horizon
the earth (in parallel to the atmosphere šw, as a location traversed by the dead king) (dated: Pyramid Texts)
[usually, in the plural] one of many gods representing forces of the earth, often imagined as serpents
flood, inundation (dated: since the Pyramid Texts)
particular point in time, moment (dated: since the Middle Kingdom)
span of time in general, time, while (dated: since the Middle Kingdom)
a small unit of time, smaller than an hour () but larger than a ; approximately a minute (dated: Greco-Roman Period)
striking power, readiness or ferocity to strike (dated: since the Pyramid Texts)
definitions.usage_notes:
While Erman and Grapow note an additional meaning of  as a ‘head ornament’, Gardiner convincingly argues that this is based on a misinterpretation of passages where it means ‘readiness to strike’. Gardiner also suggests that the ‘moment, time’ sense of  is not independent, but developed from the ‘readiness to strike’ sense by way of reference to the suddenness or speed of a strike. Allen instead takes the ‘moment’ meaning as primary, rendering the ‘readiness to strike’ sense as ‘moment of rage’.

This word is sometimes used in parallel to pḥtj. In other passages it appears in an exactly parallel context to bꜣw: compare PT 474 against PT 306 in the Pyramid Texts.

===Etymology 2===
The ''Wörterbuch'' considers this a further derived nominalized ''[[nisba]]'' adjective, presumably formed from {{af|egy|jꜣbt|gloss1=east|-j|alt2=-(j)|pos2=''[[nisba]]'' ending}}; however, the form {{m|egy||*jꜣbtj}} with the ''nisba'' ending written out is nowhere attested with this meaning. Such an analysis is, nonetheless, supported by the masculine gender of this term.

definitions.usage_notes:
The above quotes constitute all the known attestations of this word.

Allen, in his translation of the Pyramid Texts, renders this word as ‘peak’, presumably identifying it with  above. Shmakov disputes this reading and takes  as a body of water based on the determinatives and a mention of š jꜣt found in the Coffin Texts (CT III, 204f), rendering it ‘Kherti’s standard lake’, but noting that a reading ‘lower standard’ is also possible.Shmakov, Timofey T. (2012) Critical analysis of J.P. Allen’s «The Ancient Egyptian Pyramid Texts»: Preliminary Results, page 314 In this case the term would be an extended use of  above, in the role of a proper name. Shmakov notes in this regard that this word for ‘standard’ is also found written with the sign M44 in PT 254.39 (Pyr. 288c), W (see alternative forms under that term above).

definitions.usage_notes:
In Old and Middle Egyptian, this particle can stand at the beginning of adjectival, adverbial, and verbal sentences; it is followed by a nominal subject, a demonstrative pronoun, or an attached suffix pronoun. There is significant debate over what exactly it indicates in these stages of the language:
 According to Allen, it indicates that the statement in the sentence is presented as true at the time of the statement, in contrast to false statements and statements which are always or generally true. It occurs at the start of independent clauses, but never those verbal clauses beginning with an imperative, bare stative, perfective, prospective, subjunctive, biliteral suffixed (contingent), or emphatic form. It also occurs at the start of subordinate adverbial clauses if their subject is pronominal, but never if it is nominal.
 According to Loprieno, it is a ‘particle of initiality’ indicating that its sentence opens a new segment of discourse, with the semantic scope of an overt assertion of truth, and pragmatically relating the sentence to the speaker’s situation without necessarily implying direct involvement. However, in simple adverbial clauses with a pronominal subject, it can also serve as a semantically and syntactically neutral morpheme that only serves to carry an attached subject pronoun. In extremely rare cases, it can introduce the subject of an existential sentence consisting of just one element, an apparently archaic usage.
 According to Hoch, it indicates that the statement is one that the speaker wishes to present as a fact, and it only occurs in main clauses.
 It has frequently been characterized as an assertion particle, sometimes noting its apparent modal role marking realis statements.
 In the so-called Standard Theory, its role was often considered purely syntactic, marking independent clauses; this view is no longer common. Some scholars working in the frame of the Standard Theory have suggested that bare (proclitic-less) sentences following one introduced by  are main clauses that become hypotactically linked to the initial sentence in a chain of discourse, with the particle conveying the syntactic or pragmatic ‘theme’ of the whole and functioning as a nominal element.

definitions: the negative relative adjective — allows a clause to serve as a negated relative clause, usually with an adverbial or verbal predicate (dated: chiefly Old Egyptian)
definitions.usage_notes:
When  introduces an indirect relative clause with a pronominal subject, the subject generally takes the form of a suffix pronoun attached to . However, clauses with a first-person singular subject instead use the dependent pronoun wj, and those with a third-person subject sometimes use the dependent pronoun st. Other subjects can rarely also appear in dependent-pronoun form.

Properly speaking, the usage of  with a noun phrase also introduces an indirect relative clause; it constitutes the relative counterpart of a negated existential clause with nn.

Analogously to jw,  asserts that the statement in the clause is false at the time of the statement, marking it as modally realis.

===Etymology 1===
Plural form of {{m|egy|pw}}.

====Determiner====
{{egy-det|m-p|proximal, later vocative|head=i-p-w}}

# {{lb|egy|Old Egyptian}} [[these]]
# {{lb|egy|Middle Egyptian|archaizing}} [[O]] {{gloss|vocative reference}}

=====Usage notes=====
This demonstrative was originally a determiner but could later be used alone, like a pronoun. When used as a determiner it follows the noun it describes.

In Old Egyptian it forms a contrastive pair with the demonstrative {{m|egy|jpf}}, in which {{m|egy||jpw}} is [[proximal]].

Its use in Middle Egyptian texts is an archaism.

In Old Egyptian this form is also used for the dual. Traditionally this is interpreted as a summary writing of a special dual form {{m|egy|jpwj}} (attested as such only in archaizing Middle Egyptian texts). An alternative possible interpretation is that there simply was no distinction between the masculine dual and plural demonstrative determiners.

=====Inflection=====
{{Egyptian demonstratives}}

etymologies.etymology_text:
==Egyptian==

===Etymology===
From {{af|egy|jmj <t:(one) being in; interior>|wrt}}. The identity and meaning of the second term are unclear. It is written identically to {{m|egy|wrt||great one}}, but perhaps it is instead to be connected with {{m|egy|wrt||a kind of barque}}.

Any attempt to determine the etymological meaning of the term should probably take it in conjunction with its antonym {{m|egy|tꜣ wr||larboard, port}}; setting aside {{m|egy|wr}}/{{m|egy|wrt}}, here one can draw a contrast between {{m|egy|jmj}} in the one term, referring to the interior of something, and {{m|egy|tꜣ}} in the other term, apparently referring to the land exterior to the ship. For {{m|egy|tꜣ}}, compare the etymology of the English term {{m|en|port}}; because the steering oar is generally found on the right (starboard) side of the ship, it is the left (port) side that moors facing the land. It is then easy to see how the starboard side could be perceived as the ‘interior’ of the vessel, facing away from land. (Alternatively, it may be the steering oar itself that is referred to as ‘being in’ / in the ‘interior’ of the vessel.)

Thus, the term as a whole has variously been interpreted as ‘that which is inside the barque’, or, taking {{m|egy|wrt}} as ‘great one’ in reference to the ‘great oar’ (steering oar), ‘the one on the inside of the steering oar’. Servajean rejects the latter interpretation and prefers the former, as {{m|egy|wrt}} is nowhere else attested to refer to the steering oar specifically. 

===Pronunciation===
{{egy-IPA-E}}

A ‘reverse ''[[nisba]]''’ construction from {{af|egy|jmj <t:(one) being in>|r <t:mouth>}}, thus literally ‘one in whom the mouth is’, implying ‘one who gives commands’. The written form is abbreviated to omit the weak consonants.

definitions.usage_notes:
This term is usually used with a following direct genitive as part of various titles.

Titles based on  generally refer to a higher position than analogous titles with ḥrj or jrj#Noun.

===Etymology 2===
From {{af|egy|jmj <t:(one) being in>|r <t:mouth>|lit=the one in the mouth}}. The components are the same as in the etymology above, but the grammatical construction is different.

==Egyptian==

===Etymology===
{{compound|egy|jmj-r|gloss1=overseer|pr|gloss2=house}} in a direct genitive construction, thus literally ‘overseer of the house’.

===Pronunciation===
{{egy-IPA-E}}

definitions: steward; administrator of an estate/house, wealth, property, etc.

etymologies.etymology_text:

===Etymology===
From {{af|egy|jmj-r-pr <t:steward><lit:overseer of the house>|wrr <alt:wr><t:great>|lit=great overseer of the house}}.

===Pronunciation===
{{egy-IPA-E}}

From {{af|egy|jmj-r <t:overseer>|mšꜥ <t:army, workgang, expedition>}} in a direct genitive construction, thus literally ‘overseer of the army/workgang/expedition’.

===Pronunciation===
{{egy-IPA-E}}

definitions: foreman or boss of a workgang

etymologies.etymology_text:

===Etymology===
From {{af|egy|jmj <t:(one) being in>|rn <t:name>|.f <t:his>}}, a ‘reverse ''[[nisba]]''’ construction meaning ‘the one in which his name is’.

===Pronunciation===
{{egy-IPA-E}}

From {{af|egy|jmj-r <t:overseer>|ḥwt-nṯr <t:temple>}} in a direct genitive construction, thus literally ‘overseer of the temple’.

===Pronunciation===
{{egy-IPA-E}}

===Etymology===
{{compound|egy|jmj-r|gloss1=overseer|šnwt|gloss2=granary}} in a direct genitive construction, thus literally ‘overseer of the granary’.

===Pronunciation===
{{egy-IPA-E}}

{{egy-IPA-E}}

etymologies.etymology_text:

===Etymology===
From {{af|egy|jmj <t:(one) being in>|ḫt <t:what is behind or after>}}. The [[nisba]] equivalent to {{m|egy|m ḫt}}.

===Pronunciation===

[usually, in the plural] successor, descendant, aftercomer, one who will come after; [in the plural] posterity

etymologies.etymology_text:
==Egyptian==

===Etymology===
From {{af|egy|jmj <t:(one) being in>|sꜣ <t:back>|lit=the one in the back}}. Other interpretations have also been suggested, for example taking the second term as {{m|egy|zꜣ||protection}} or {{m|egy|zꜣ||phyle, troop}}.

===Pronunciation===
{{egy-IPA-E}}

definitions: helper, acolyte, functionary; also used as a title
a kind of heart-shaped piece of jewelry

etymologies.etymology_text:
==Egyptian==

===Etymology===
From {{af|egy|jmj <t:(one) being in>|tꜣ <t:earth>|lit=the one in the earth}}. Compare the non-titular use of the plural form {{m|egy|jmw tꜣ||snakes; rocks|lit=those in the earth}}.

===Pronunciation===
{{egy-IPA-E}}

==Egyptian==

===Etymology===
Probably originally a derivative of {{m|egy|m||in}}; compare {{m|egy|jmj||being in}}.

===Pronunciation===
{{egy-IPA-E}}

definitions: [with a dual object or two objects separated by ] between
[with a plural object] among, amidst, in the midst of

etymologies.etymology_text:

===Etymology===
The adverbial form of {{m|egy|jmjtw}}, from {{af|egy|jmjtw <t:between, among>|nj <t:thereto, for it>}}.

===Pronunciation===
{{egy-IPA-E}}

===Etymology===
{{af|egy|jmj|t1=being in|dwꜣt|t2=afterworld}}, thus ‘(that which) is in the afterworld’.

===Pronunciation===

===Pronunciation===

etymologies.etymology_text:
==Egyptian==

===Etymology===
Possibly related to {{m|egy|jm||a kind of material}}.

===Pronunciation===
{{egy-IPA-E}}

definitions.usage_notes:
This word is found on the Stele of Irtysen (Louvre C 14), line 11; another possible attestation on pBM EA 10735 is debated, with the Thesaurus Linguae Aegyptiae instead reading it as jmt-kꜣp.

The second glyph of the word is unclear; Faulkner and the Wörterbuch silently correct it to , but in the original text it is more sickle-shaped and opens upward. The slip from which the Wörterbuch entry was compiled notes that it ought to be  based on its position and size.

definitions: boat, ship in general (dated: Old Kingdom to New Kingdom)
lamentation, wail, cry of mourning (dated: since the Middle Kingdom)
contents of an abscess or boil; pus (dated: Medical papyri)

etymologies.etymology_text:
==Egyptian==

===Etymology===
From the plural of {{m|egy|jmj ḥꜣt||(one) being in front or earlier in time; anterior (one)}}, equivalent to {{af|egy|jmj <t:(one) being in>|-w <pos:plural suffix>|ḥꜣt <t:front>}}.

===Pronunciation===
{{egy-IPA-E}}

definitions: [plural only] forebears, ancestors, those of times gone by
[plural only] lesser gods who walk in front of a chief god (dated: Greco-Roman Period)

etymologies.etymology_text:
==Egyptian==

===Etymology===
From {{af|egy|jmj <alt:jmw><t:(those) being in>|tꜣ <t:earth>|lit=those in the earth}}. Compare the singular form {{m|egy|jmj-tꜣ}}, used as a priestly title.

===Pronunciation===
{{egy-IPA-E}}

alternative_forms.hieroglyphs: imi-m-w-Z3-tA:N23*Z1<!--following the Wörterbuch lemma, but is it actually attested?-->

definitions: Alternative form of jmjtw (dated: Old Kingdom)

pronunciations: q=proper noun|o=jaˈmaːnuw|m=jaˈmaːnuw|ml=ʔaˈmaːnə|l=ʔaˈmoːn|onote=<ref>Schenkel, Wolfgang (1990) ''Einführung in die altägyptische Sprachwissenschaft'', page 89</ref>

definitions: [transitive, or, reflexive] to hide, to conceal, to make secret (+ r: from (someone); + m: in (something))
[intransitive] to hide, to be(come) hidden or secret
[intransitive, by extension] to be(come) rare or precious (dated: Greco-Roman Period)
[transitive] to create, form, shape (in a cosmic, divine sense) (dated: Pyramid Texts and 18th Dynasty)
definitions.usage_notes: Often used with a following noun to mean ‘one who/which hides…’, ‘one with a hidden…’.

definitions: an epithet of various gods: hidden one, secret one
a priestly title: hidden one, secret one (dated: Greco-Roman Period)
Amun, a primeval god, personification of the hiddenness of the primeval waters, worshipped at Hermopolis as a member of the Ogdoad (dated: since the Pyramid Texts)
Amun, a god worshipped at Thebes as a member of the Theban Triad, and seen as the king of the gods (dated: since the Middle Kingdom)
a minor god in the form of a snake worshipped at Prosopis and Thebes (dated: Theban Royal Tombs and Greco-Roman Period)

definitions.usage_notes: This word was chiefly used in very old texts, and early on replaced by wnmj.

definitions: : abode, place of stay (dated: Pyramid Texts)

etymologies.etymology_text:
==Egyptian==

===Etymology===
From {{af|egy|jmn <t:[[Amun]]>|jpt <t:Luxor, inner sanctum>}} in a direct genitive construction, thus “Amun of Luxor”, “Amun of the inner sanctum”.

===Pronunciation===
{{egy-IPA-E}}

==Egyptian==

===Etymology===
From {{af|egy|jmn <t:hidden>|ꜥ <t:arm>}} in a direct genitive construction, thus literally “hidden of arm”, i.e. “(the one) with the hidden arm”.

===Pronunciation===
{{egy-IPA-E}}

definitions: a priestly title for a priest of Bastet (dated: Late Period)

etymologies.etymology_text:
==Egyptian==

===Etymology===
From {{af|egy|jmn <t:[[Amun]]>|m <t:in>|jpt <t:Luxor, inner sanctum>}}, thus “Amun in Luxor”, “Amun in the inner sanctum”. The personal name is probably to be interpreted as an adverbial sentence, “Amun is in Luxor”.

===Pronunciation===
{{egy-IPA-E}}

definitions: the form of the god Amun worshipped at Luxor (dated: since the 18th Dynasty)
the form of the god Amun worshipped at Karnak (dated: since the 18th Dynasty)

pronunciations: o=jaˌmaːnuw ma ˈħuːʀit|m=jaˌmaːnuw mə ˈħuːʀiʔ|ml=ʔaˌmaːnə məˈħuːʔə|l=ʔaˌmoːn əmˈħeːʔ

etymologies.etymology_text:
==Egyptian==

===Etymology===
From {{af|egy|jmn <t:[[Amun]]>|msj <alt:ms><t:to give birth>|.w <alt:(.w)><pos:masculine third-person singular stative ending>}}, thus ‘Amun is born’.

===Pronunciation===
{{egy-IPA-E}}

==Egyptian==

===Etymology===
From {{af|egy|jmn <t:[[Amun]]>|nḫt <t:strong, victorious>|.w <alt:(.w)><pos:masculine singular stative ending>}}, thus ‘[[Amun]] is strong’.

===Pronunciation===
{{egy-IPA-E}}

==Egyptian==

===Etymology===
From {{af|egy|jmn <t:hidden>|nṯr <alt:nṯrw><t:gods>}} in a direct genitive construction, thus literally “hidden of the gods”, i.e. “most hidden one among the gods”, “most hidden god”.

===Pronunciation===
{{egy-IPA-E}}

definitions: an epithet for various gods (dated: Theban Royal Tombs and Greco-Roman Period)
the god Amun-Ra (dated: since the 18th Dynasty)
c. 1450 , The Poetical Stela of Thutmose III, Part I (Cairo Museum 34010):Middle Egyptian Grammar: The Poetical Stela of Thutmose III: Part I , Dr. Gabor Toth, Rutgers University.

etymologies.etymology_text:
==Egyptian==

===Etymology===
From {{af|egy|jmn <t:hidden>|rn <t:name>}} in a direct genitive construction, thus literally ‘hidden of name’, i.e. ‘he whose name is hidden’.

===Pronunciation===
{{egy-IPA-E}}

definitions: a minor god mentioned in old religious texts (dated: Pyramid Texts and Coffin Texts)
definitions.usage_notes: Distinct from jmn-rn.f, which is an epithet for other gods, particularly Amun.

etymologies.etymology_text:
==Egyptian==

===Etymology===
From {{af|egy|jmn <t:hidden>|rn <t:name>|.f <t:his>}} in a direct genitive construction, thus literally ‘Hidden of his Name’, i.e. ‘he whose name is hidden’.

===Pronunciation===
{{egy-IPA-E}}

definitions: an epithet of the god Amun, occasioanlly also used of other gods
definitions.usage_notes: Distinct from jmn-rn, which is the name of a particular minor god mentioned in the Pyramid Texts and Coffin Texts.

definitions: [Egyptian mythology] Amenhotep (son of Hapu), a deified scribe and architect

Amaunet, a primeval goddess, female personification of the hiddenness of the primeval waters (as a counterpart to the male Amun), worshipped at Hermopolis as a member of the Ogdoad (dated: since the Pyramid Texts)
Amaunet, a goddess worshipped at Thebes as the female counterpart of the king of the gods Amun (dated: since the Middle Kingdom)

etymologies.etymology_text:
==Egyptian==

===Etymology===
Feminine form of the more common {{m|egy|jmj wrt||starboard}}, formed with the addition of the feminine ending {{af|egy|-t}} to the [[nisba]] {{m|egy|jmj}}. See {{m|egy|jmj wrt}} for further etymology. Equivalent to {{af|egy|jmj <alt:jmt>|wrt}}.

===Pronunciation===
{{egy-IPA-E}}

==Egyptian==

===Etymology===
A nominalized ''[[nisba]]'' adjective in a reverse ''nisba'' construction, {{compound|egy|jmj|alt1=jmt|gloss1=being in|pr|gloss2=house, estate}}, literally ‘what the estate is in’.

===Pronunciation===
{{egy-IPA-E}}

definitions: inventory of a house’s or estate’s property and goods
specifically, such property as a bequeathed legacy or estate; bequest

==Egyptian==

===Etymology===
Feminine form of {{m|egy|jmj ḥꜣt||(one) being in front or earlier in time; anterior (one)}}, formed with the addition of the feminine ending {{af|egy|-t}} to the [[nisba]] {{m|egy|jmj}}. Equivalent to {{af|egy|jmj <alt:jmj><t:(one) being in>|-t <pos:feminine ending>|ḥꜣt <t:front>}}.

{{egy-IPA-E}}

==Egyptian==

===Etymology===
From {{af|egy|jmj <alt:jmt><pos:feminine of {{m|egy|jmj||(one) being in}}>|ḥꜣt <t:front>|.f <t:his>|lit=she who is in his front}}.

===Pronunciation===
{{egy-IPA-E}}

definitions.usage_notes:
This particle comes at the beginning of an interrogative sentence. It can be used alongside the interrogative particle tr or by itself as the sole such particle.

In adverbial sentences with , the particle jw regularly follows , and nominal sentences with  can also have it followed by jw. Verb forms that use  as an initial particle in main clauses also usually have  followed by jw in yes/no questions.

definitions: introduces the agent of a passive construction, when not a personal pronoun; by
introduces the agent of an infinitive, when not a personal pronoun
introduces an emphasized subject (one that serves as the rheme of the clause), when not a personal pronoun
definitions.usage_notes:
Introduces the subject or topic of the sentence. The agent it introduces cannot be a personal pronoun.

Allen considers this preposition to be ‘probably the same word’ as the above interrogative particle.

etymologies.etymology_text:
===Etymology 2===
{{univerbation|egy}} of {{af|egy|j|t1=to say|.w|alt2=(.w)|pos2=third-person masculine singular stative ending|jn|t3=by|pos3=the preposition above}}. The feminine form is a univerbation of {{af|egy|j|t1=to say|.tj|alt2=.t(j)|pos2=third-person feminine singular stative ending|jn|t3=by|pos3=the preposition above}}, and the plural and dual are derived from the perfect of the verb {{m|egy|j||to say}} with a third-person plural or dual suffix pronoun ({{m|egy|.sn}} or {{m|egy|.snj}}, respectively).

====Pronunciation====
{{egy-IPA-E}}

definitions: [with following noun indicating the speaker] marks a non-future direct quotation; says, said
definitions.usage_notes:
Like the other quotatives kꜣ, ḫr, and ḫrw.fj, this word either follows the entire quotation that it marks or is inserted near its start (but never at its start).

This quotative is common in Old and Late Egyptian but restricted to archaic religious texts in Middle Egyptian.

etymologies.etymology_text:
===Etymology 2===
{{unc|egy}}. Like many fifth-dynasty pharaohs’ birth names, this name may simply be a diminutive without any meaning of its own, perhaps of the pharaoh’s throne name {{m|egy|n-wsr-rꜥ}} (in which case it may not be the actual name given at birth). Alternatively, some have tentatively attempted to explain it with various meanings, such as ‘the delayed one’ or ‘the (one with the bushy?) eyebrows’.

====Pronunciation====

==Egyptian==

===Etymology===
{{unc|egy}}. Like many fifth-dynasty pharaohs’ birth names, this name may simply be a diminutive without any meaning of its own, perhaps of the pharaoh’s throne name {{m|egy|mn-kꜣw-ḥr}} (in which case it may not be the actual name given at birth).

===Pronunciation===
{{egy-IPA-E|ang=jkꜣw-ḥor}}

==Egyptian==

===Etymology===
Compare the earlier {{cog|egy-mid|jkn||cup}}, but also (separately) {{cog|he|אַגָּן|tr=ʾaggā́n||ritual- or banquet-bowl}}, {{cog|phn|𐤀𐤂𐤍||bowl}}, {{cog|uga|𐎀𐎂𐎐||basin}}, Warka {{cog|arc|tr=ag-gan-nu}}, {{m|arc|tr=ag-ga-nu||t=basin or bowl}}, {{cog|jpa|גָנייא דקדשׁ||basins of Qadesh}}, {{cog|syc|ܐܓܢܐ|tr=ʾaggānā||water pitcher}}, {{cog|ar|إجّانَة||large bowl}}, {{cog|akk||ts=agannu||large bowl of copper or silver}}. The equivalent of the Egyptian term is also attested in cuneiform transcription in the Amarna letters as {{m|akk|tr=a-ku-nu|ts=akūnu}}, with Albright, Lambdin, and the ''Chicago Assyrian Dictionary'' claiming this to be Egyptian in origin; Hoch argues that the reverse is true, and Egyptian borrowed the word from {{bor|egy|sem}}. In Egyptian, the word appears in lists of items from Syria-Palestine, while in the Amarna letters the word appears in lists of items sent from Egypt; the word is, however, much more widely attested in Semitic languages than in Egyptian. Hoch consequently thinks that the direction of borrowing was into Egyptian, and that the word may not be connected with {{cog|egy-mid|jkn||cup}}.

===Pronunciation===

===Etymology===
Schneider reconstructs the name as {{der|egy|sem-nwe}} ''*ʾadōnī-rōʿē-yāh'', "My lord is the shepherd of [[Yah]]"; both Schneider and Shalomi Hen identify ''*-yāh'' with an abbreviated form of the toponym {{m|egy|yhwꜣ}}, attested to during the 13th century BCE, whose relationship to the theonym [[Yahweh]] is still debated. Schneider takes the phrase ''*rōʿē-yāh'' as a whole as a divine [[epithet]] for Yahweh in his association with the toponym.

==Egyptian==

===Etymology===
A compound of {{compound|egy|ywd|gloss1=hand, monument|mꜥrwk|alt2=(h)mꜥrwk|gloss2=king}} in a direct genitive construction, thus literally ‘Monument of the King’. Both components are borrowings from {{bor|egy|sem}}, ultimately from {{cog|sem-pro|*yad-}} and {{m|sem-pro|*malk-}}; it may be the entire place name was directly borrowed from Semitic. The {{m|egy||h}} in the Egyptian form reflects a Semitic definite article: compare {{cog|he|הַ־}}.

Earlier hypotheses interpreting the word as ‘king of [[Judah]]’ are now largely rejected.

definitions.usage_notes:
For expressing general or gnomic statements,  is used in the perfective, unlike other verbs, which are used in the imperfective for this function.

As  has no perfect form, it uses the perfective in situations where the perfect might otherwise be expected.

Existential clauses are formed with  in the perfective, typically beginning with jw  for positive existential clauses or nn  for negative existential clauses. The negative can also be introduced with the terminative nj  (usually in dependent clauses) or jwt  (usually in noun clauses). Yes-no questions about existence are generally introduced with jn jw .

When  is used in an inflected form of the suffix conjugation or as a verbal adjective, it can effectively make adverbial predicates (including verbs in the stative) in its clause have the meaning or function of that inflected form, e.g.  in the subjunctive can give an adverbial predicate a subjunctive meaning or function. Thus, it also allows them to form:
 causatives with rḏj, by having a subjunctive wn be the object of rḏj with a following adverbial/stative predicate.
 the protasis of a conditional sentence, by having a prospective wnn follow jr with a following adverbial/stative predicate.

etymologies.etymology_text:
==Egyptian==

===Etymology===
Several proposals have been made for the etymology and meaning of the original name; as Smith (2017) notes, none are fully convincing.<ref name="Smith">Smith, Mark (2017) ''Following Osiris: Perspectives on the Osirian Afterlife from Four Millennia'', pages 124–126, 372–389</ref> Most take {{m|egy||wsjr}} as the accepted transliteration, following Adolf Erman:

* Griffiths (1980), “bearing in mind Erman’s emphasis on the fact that the name must begin with an [sic] ''w''”, proposes a derivation from {{m|egy|wsr}} with an original meaning of “The Mighty One”.<ref name="Griffiths">Griffiths, John Gwyn (1980) ''The Origins of Osiris and His Cult''</ref>
* Sethe (1930) proposes a compound {{m|egy|st}}-{{m|egy|jrt}}, meaning “seat of the eye”, in a hypothetical earlier form {{m|egy||*wst-jrt}}; this is rejected by Griffiths on phonetic grounds.<ref name="Griffiths" />
* Lorton (1985) takes up a similar compound but explains {{m|egy|st}}-{{m|egy|jrj|jrt}} as signifying “product, something made”, from the verb {{m|egy|jrj}}, with Osiris representing the product of the mummification process.<ref>Lorton, David (1985) in ''Varia Aegyptiaca I'', pages 117–121</ref>
* Westendorf (1987) proposes an etymology from {{m|egy|wꜣst}}-{{m|egy|jrt}} “she who bears the eye”.<ref>Westendorf, Wolfhart (1987) “Zur Etymologie des Namens Osiris: ''*wꜣs.t-jr.t'' “die das Auge trägt”.” in J. Osing and G. Dreyer (editors), ''Form und Mass: Beiträge zur Literatur, Sprache und Kunst des alten Ägypten: Festschrift für Gerhard Fecht zum 65. Geburtstag am 6. Februar 1987'', pages 456–461</ref>
* Zeidler (2000) reviews the common hypotheses and rejects the interpretation of the second element as either {{m|egy|jrj||to do, make}} or {{m|egy|jrt||eye}} on phonetic grounds, ultimately agreeing with Griffiths on the meaning and rendering the name {{m|egy|wsrw|(w)sr(w)}} with the assumption that the writing of the name reflects an archaic use of the throne and eye hieroglyphs as uniliteral signs.<ref>Zeidler, Jürgen (2000) “Zur Etymologie des Gottesnamens Osiris” in ''Studien zur Altägyptischen Kultur'', volume 28, pages 309–316</ref>
* Smith (2017) makes no definitive proposals but asserts that the second element must be a form of {{m|egy|jrj||to do, make}} (rather than {{m|egy|jrt||eye}}), since the word is found complemented with {{m|egy||r}} in writings of the Middle Kingdom.<ref name="Smith" />

However, recently alternative transliterations have been proposed:

* Muchiki (1990) reexamines Erman’s evidence that the throne hieroglyph in the word is to be read {{m|egy||ws}} and finds it unconvincing, suggesting instead that the name should be read {{m|egy|ꜣsjr}} on the basis of Aramaic, Phoenician, and Old South Arabian transcriptions, readings of the throne sign in other words, and comparison with {{m|egy|ꜣst||Isis}}.<ref>Muchiki, Yoshi (1990) “On the transliteration of the name Osiris” in ''The Journal of Egyptian Archaeology'', volume 76, pages 191–194</ref>
* Allen (2010) reads the word as {{m|egy|jsjrt}} but later revises the reading (2013) to {{m|egy|jsjrj}} and derives it from {{m|egy|js}}-{{m|egy|jrj}}, meaning “engendering (male) principle”.<ref>Allen, James P. (2013) “The Name of Osiris (and Isis)” in ''Lingua Aegyptia'', volume 21, pages 9–14.</ref>

{{wikipedia|Osiris}}
[[Image:Osiris_bookofthedead.JPG|thumb|right|180px|<hiero>Q1:ir-A40</hiero>]]

===Pronunciation===
{{egy-IPA-E}}

definitions: [in funerary literature] conventionally appended before the name of the deceased: Osirian form of a dead person, deceased person as Osiris (see usage notes)
definitions.usage_notes: As a designation for the deceased, this word has traditionally been interpreted as standing in apposition to the dead person’s name, identifying them with the god Osiris: ‘the Osiris N.N.’ However, a variant form of this construction with the word nj inserted between the two elements is attested since the Coffin Texts. This suggests the version where the two are juxtaposed is in fact a direct genitive construction meaning ‘the Osiris of N.N.’, not an apposition. Smith suggests that the meaning of ‘the Osiris of’ a dead person was ‘the form that an individual acquired as a result of the rites of mummification and justification’, at the end of which ‘they could be said to possess an Osiris-aspect’, an ‘Osirian form’ unique to each individual and not to be directly identified with the god Osiris.

[[File:AncientEgyptianRelief-BeeHieroglyph-ROM.png|thumb|265x265px|Bee hieroglyph from the tomb complex of Senusret I (d. 1,926 BC)]]

Heavily disputed. The final {{m|egy|-t}} is usually considered a separate feminine ending in origin rather than a part of the root, but this is not wholly certain. Etymological hypotheses include:
* Cognate with {{cog|bej|wíyu}}.
* From an earlier form *''brt'', in which case there are a number of mutually exclusive possibilities:
** Cognate with {{cog|elo|póruat||bee}}.
** Cognate with Western Rift *''baʾara'' (“bee”) and its descendants: {{cog|irk|baʾārmō||bee}}, {{cog|bds|băʾălĭmŭ||bee}}, {{cog|wbj|baʾaramo||fly, bee}}.
** Cognate with {{cog|mif|béber||horsefly}}.
** Cognate with {{cog|lme|b̰úr||honey (?)}}
* From an earlier form *''blt'', cognate with {{cog|kul|ʾabyál||honey}}, {{cog|dkx|bŏlŏ́m||honey}}, {{cog|mse|mbulyuma||honey}}, {{cog|lln|bùlò||hive}}.
Several linguists have also proposed an areal connection with {{cog|ine-pro|*bʰey-||bee}}, noting the existence of a number of parallels between Afroasiatic and Indo-European bee-keeping terminology.

====Usage notes====
This demonstrative was originally a determiner but could later be used alone, like a pronoun. When used as a determiner it follows the noun it describes.

When used in nominal sentences, {{m|egy||pw}} does not vary by the gender or number of the referent; it is used with nouns and pronouns of any gender or number.

In Old Egyptian this form was occasionally used in place of the plural {{m|egy|jpw}} (and at least once for the dual {{m|egy|jpwj}}). Whether this should be interpreted as a mere summarily written variant of {{m|egy|jpw}} or as a genuine use of the singular for the plural is unclear.

===Etymology 1===
Most likely {{onomatopoeic|egy|nocap=1}}, from the animal’s cry ([[meow]]). Compare {{cog|zh|貓|tr=māo}}, {{cog|lo|ແມວ}}.

Other hypotheses connect it to {{cog|afa-pro|*m-r}} or {{m|afa-pro|*m-l}}, the former on the basis of {{cog|wbj|mariy-amo||wild cat}}, Lamé {{cog|nnn|mēr||serval}} and {{m|nnn|méríán||wild cat}}, {{cog|lme|merian||wild cat, serval}}, Zime-Dari {{cog|lme|mīēr||genette}}, and the latter on the basis of {{cog|mug|ámíl||African civet}}, Bedanga {{cog|sok|melā||cat}}. Either one of these could also be plausibly connected with the ancestor of {{cog|egy|mꜣj||lion}}.

etymologies.etymology_text:
===Etymology 1===
Unclear. Presumably consisting of the unattested root ''*ꜥbr'' with [[prefix]] ''m-''. 

Semantically, this word might have originally referred to a “[[lunar month]] of thirty days” as suggested by A. Ember (1926); cf. {{ncog|jbn|u-yěr||moon; thirty}}. Based on this, Takacs (2007) compares the root ''*ꜥbr'' ~ ''*ꜥrb'' (via [[metathesis]]) to Proto-Agaw ''*ʔärb-'' ~ ''ʔärf-'' ("moon"), and further to {{der|egy|sem-pro|*ʿ-r-p|t=cloud}} (whence {{cog|he|ערפל}}).<ref>{{R:egy:EDE|v=3|p=176}}</ref>

etymologies.etymology_text:
===Etymology 3===
{{etymid|egy|pyramid}}
Highly disputed etymology. Hypotheses include:
* From {{inh|egy|afa-pro|-}}, cognate with {{cog|ar|أَمَرَة|t=heap of stones, mound, esp. as a way-marker}}, {{cog|akk|𒀯|t=dividing wall|tr=amartu}}, {{m|akk|𒋞|t=pile of bricks|tr=amaru}}, {{cog|he|אָמִיר|t=treetop, mountain summit|tr=ʾāmīr}}.
* Metathesized from earlier {{m|egy||*rm}}, from {{inh|egy|afa-pro|*rim-|t=to be raised, high, long}}, cognate with {{cog|sem-pro|*rayam-|t=to be high}}; compare {{cog|ar|رَيْم|t=abundance, hill, tumulus, step}}
* From a possible {{inh|egy|afa-pro|*m-r|t=heap of stones}}, cognate with {{cog|shi|i-miri|t=heap of stones, wall of dry stone}}, {{m|shi|a-mra|t=stone buttress of a terraced field}}, {{cog|tzm|i-mr-an|t=large half-buried stones that mark off property boundaries}}, {{cog|mif|mémeré|t=low stone terrace wall}}.
* Related to a Semitic root {{m|sem-pro|*m-w-r}}, as in {{cog|xqt|𐩣𐩥𐩧𐩩𐩬|t=tower|tr=mwrtn}}, {{cog|ar|مَارَ|t=to come to a high place or plateau}}.

etymologies.etymology_text:
==Egyptian==

===Etymology===
From {{af|egy|mḏd|t1=to strike true, to stay true to, to drive in, to share out, to impose as an obligation|-w}}. The exact sense is disputed, with a number of proposed hypotheses, but it must certainly be related to Khufu’s Two Ladies name {{m|egy|mḏd-r-nbtj}}, itself of disputed interpretation. Baud takes the term as an active participle synonymous with the epithet {{m|egy|šzp-mḏd.f||(he who) receives his dues}}, or alternatively suggests an interpretation such as ‘he who reaches the goal’, but rejects earlier suggestions by Montet (‘he who imposes’), Sethe (‘faithful, attached’), Barta (‘he who is guided, directed’), and Gundlach (‘he who shares out’). Leprohon interprets it as a passive participle, ‘[he] who has been adhered to/followed’ (= ‘stayed true to’).

===Pronunciation===

==Egyptian==

===Etymology===
From {{af|egy|mḏd|t1=to strike true, to stay true to, to drive in, to share out, to impose as an obligation|r|t2=concerning, according to, facing, against, etc.|nbtj|t3=the Two Ladies, i.e. the goddesses Nekhbet and Wadjet}}. The exact sense is disputed, with a number of proposed hypotheses, but it must certainly be related to Khufu’s serekh name {{m|egy|mḏdw}}, itself of disputed interpretation; a phrase attested in the Coffin Texts CT VI, §307x–308b, may also feature a related construction: {{m|egy|[[jn]] [{{l|en|N.N.}}] [[jrj|jr]] [[mḏdt|mḏdwt]] [[nbtj]]||It was [{{l|en|N.N.}}] who undertook the sharing out of the two crowns {{qlit|Two Ladies}}}}. Gundlach proposed a meaning of ‘he who shares out in accordance with the Two Ladies’, which Baud rejected in favor of ‘he who receives his dues in accordance with the Two Ladies’. Leprohon instead suggested ‘[he] who has adhered to the Two Ladies’, though this interpretation leaves the preposition unexplained, as {{m|egy|mḏd}} normally takes the thing being stayed true to as a direct object.

===Pronunciation===
{{egy-IPA-E}}

When used in this way, it precedes the noun, with the genitival adjective nj in between, e.g. "said feet" is  (literally "the aforementioned one of feet").

In Middle Egyptian, this pronoun is somewhat colloquial; in Late Egyptian its force has weakened to that of a definite article.
This demonstrative was primarily a determiner but could also be used alone, as a pronoun. When used as a determiner it precedes the noun it describes.

definitions.usage_notes:
This genitival adjective can be used to express the indirect genitive. In this case, it indicates that the noun preceding it, with which it agrees in gender and number, is possessed by the noun which follows it.

In Late Egyptian the functional contrasts of characterization versus specification that distinguished the indirect and direct genitive disappeared, and outside a restricted set of particular words the indirect genitive with  largely supplanted the direct genitive without it.

etymologies.etymology_text:
===Etymology 2===
Oréal hypothesizes that {{m|egy||nj}} originated as a verb expressing nonexistence or absence in a stative construction, drawing a speculative connection with the attested verb {{m|egy|nj||to rebuff, to drive away}}.<ref>Oréal, Elsa (2022) “The negative existential cycle in Ancient Egyptian” in Ljuba Veselinova & Arja Hamari (eds.), ''The Negative Existential Cycle'', Berlin: Language Science Press, pages 197–230</ref>

A cognate relation to {{cog|sem-pro|*lā||no, not}} has also been suggested.

definitions: [Old Egyptian, with a following noun or pronoun] there is no, there are no; introduces an independent negated existential clause
[Middle Egyptian] not; negates a nominal sentence, an adjectival sentence of possession, or the rheme of an emphatic clause (used with js; see Usage Notes below)

[Middle Egyptian] not; negates most verbal predicates besides infinitival, imperative, and subjunctive forms; forms the negation of the perfect, perfect passive, terminative, perfective, imperfective, prospective, and prospective passive.
no, not any; negates an individual noun
definitions.usage_notes:
When used alone,  negates the individual word or verbal predicate following it.

 When negating (nonverbal) nominal sentences, adjectival sentences of possession (which start with the genitival adjective nj n), and rhemes of emphatic clauses, this particle is typically followed by the first element of the negated clause and then the negative particle js. In Middle Egyptian it cannot negate adjectival sentences which do not indicate possession, nor adverbial sentences, which are instead negated by nn. It also cannot negate verbal sentences that are not emphatic, so the presence of a verb between  and js always indicates an emphatic clause.

  combines with a number of other words to form negative particles with more specialised meanings, for which see the next section.

This demonstrative is a pronoun, and so does not directly modify nouns. In Middle Egyptian it becomes used as a demonstrative for plural nouns in place of the old adjectives jpw and jptw and comes to serve as a plural definite article. When used in this way, it precedes the noun, with the genitival adjective nj in between, e.g. "these feet" is  (literally "this of feet").

In Old Egyptian it forms a contrastive pair with the demonstrative pronoun nf, in which  is proximal.

definitions.usage_notes: There is some disagreement about how to read this word and its ideogram ; the German tradition (cf. the Wörterbuch) tends to read nt or , while Loprieno reads nt with an unwritten but phonemic glottal stop, and the Anglo-American tradition (cf. Gardiner, Allen, Faulkner) reads njwt. Gardiner supports the latter reading with reference to  nwtjw from the Pyramid Texts, derived from njwt. The German readings are supported by a writing of  for the name of the goddess Tefnut (tfnwt or tfnt) in the Amduat IV 48, as well as by the use of the word in place of  in writings of ḥnt. The reading of  is apparently supported by Diodorus Siculus, who claims that Thebes  was named after Osiris’s mother, presumably the goddess Nut (). Loprieno’s reading with a glottal stop is supported by the Hebrew rendering נֹא of the name of Thebes as well as its Akkadian transcription 𒉌𒀪. Other evidence includes the very late variant writing  nwtkꜣrṯ for Ancient Greek Ναύκρατις and the (late) Greek rendering of the word as  in the name of the pharaoh Psusennes.

From {{af|egy|nb <t:lord>|rꜥ <t:sun, Ra>}}. The exact meaning of this is debated, as there are several possible ways to interpret the name:

===Etymology===
The reading and interpretation of this name are disputed. Depending on the presence or absence of [[honorific transposition]], {{m|egy|rꜥ}} may be read as either following or preceding {{m|egy||nfr.f}}. Furthermore, it is unclear if the {{m|egy||f}} in this name is to be read as a suffix pronoun {{m|egy|.f||he, his}} or simply a phonetic complement to the sign for {{m|egy|nfr}}. Verner has proposed that the name was originally intended to be read as {{m|egy|rꜥ-nfr||Ra is beautiful}} but was soon misconstrued as {{m|egy|rꜥ-nfr.f||Ra, he is beautiful}}. Leprohon accepts this idea of a later misconstrual but reads the name with {{m|egy|rꜥ}} at the end, so that the king’s name does not focus on the sun god but rather on the king himself; he proposes an analysis following the sequence of {{af|egy|nfr <t:to be pleasing, fine, good>|.f <t:he>|rꜥ <t:Ra>}}, thus ‘he is perfect [= fine] (in the manner of) Ra’ (from an original form {{m|egy|nfr-rꜥ||the perfection of Ra}}).

When negating an adverbial or adjectival sentence, this particle stands near the beginning of the negated sentence, before the subject, but it can be preceded by other particles. It is followed by a nominal subject, a demonstrative pronoun, or a dependent pronoun as subject.

 When (exceptionally) negating a nominal sentence, this particle either pairs with the particle js like the ordinary negative particle for nominal sentences, nj, or simply stands by itself at the beginning of the sentence.

definitions.usage_notes: Though a noun in Egyptian, this word frequently describes another noun by serving as the first element in an indirect genitive construction with nj (thus literally “some of”), and it is often best translated into English as a determiner. Less commonly, it may be linked to the following noun with the preposition m. In either case,  is typically used with a singular noun in Old and Middle Egyptian, while in Late Egyptian the accompanying noun may also be plural.

the relative adjective — allows a clause to serve as a relative clause, usually with an adverbial or verbal predicate
definitions.usage_notes:
When followed by an indirect relative clause with a pronominal subject, the subject takes the form of a suffix pronoun attached to ; in this case  is often written without the two strokes representing final . The exceptions to this are clauses with a first-person singular subject, which use the dependent pronoun wj, and sometimes a third-person subject, which can use the dependent pronoun st. Other subjects rarely also appear in dependent-pronoun form.

When a direct relative clause is negated, it is given an explicit resumptive subject pronoun after the negative particle rather than having  serve in place of a subject. Alternatively, jwtj can be used instead of  and a negative particle.

Like jw,  asserts that the statement in the clause is true at the time of the statement, marking it as modally realis.

==Egyptian==

===Etymology===
From {{af|egy|nt <t:Neith>|ḥtp <t:to be content>}}. The interpretation is unclear; a reading as ‘Neith is content’ in this order does not seem possible: if {{m|egy|ḥtp}} were in the stative, it would need the feminine stative ending {{m|egy|.tj}} rather than an unwritten masculine stative ending, and in any case theophoric names using the stative did not appear until the Middle Kingdom. A solution may be found in [[honorific transposition]], in which case the intended reading would be {{m|egy|ḥtp-nt}}. Indeed, just such a name is attested in later times.

==Egyptian==

===Etymology===
{{af|egy|nṯr|t1=god|nfr|t2=pleasing, fine, good, beautiful}}, thus ‘the pleasing/fine/good/beautiful god’. The use of the term in contrast with {{m|egy|nṯr-ꜥꜣ||the elder god}} shows that the implication of {{m|egy|nfr}} here was probably one of youthful beauty or, euphemistically, simply youth, as also seen in {{m|egy|nfrt||young woman}}. A rendering such as ‘the youthful god’ is thus perhaps truer to the intended meaning than the traditional rendering ‘the good god’.<ref>On the meaning and translation of this term see also especially the discussion in Berlev, Oleg (2003) “Два Царя — Два Солнца: К мировоззрению древних египтян” and the translated version “Two kings – Two Suns: On the Worldview of the Ancient Egyptians” in ''Discovering Egypt from the Neva: the Egyptological Legacy of Oleg D. Berlev'', edited by Quirke, Stepehen, Berlin: Achet-Verlag, pages 1–35</ref>

definitions.usage_notes:
In the Old Kingdom, this word was consistently masculine and usually distinct in its singular and plural forms. By the Middle Kingdom, its final consonant changed to , with the consequence that the word changed genders to become feminine, and the singular was no longer typically distinguished in writing from its plural form. The written form from this time on occasionally included both the old and new consonants as rmṯt. Before the beginning of the New Kingdom, syllable-final  was lost throughout Egyptian, and in Late Egyptian the word returned to being masculine.Uljas, Sami (2022) “The Destruction of ‘Mankind’” in Zeitschrift für Ägyptische Sprache und Altertumskunde, volume 149, issue 2, pages 274–280

For many years Egyptologists distinguished this word as a masculine noun in its sense of ‘person’, etc., from a supposedly separate feminine collective term rmṯt; it is now clear the two words are one and the same, with the different written forms resulting from attempts to render the changing pronunciation (and gender) of the word as the final consonant first became  and then was elided entirely.

etymologies.etymology_text:
==Egyptian==

===Etymology===
If {{m|egy||pr.n}} is the perfect form of {{m|egy|prj}}, the name consists of {{af|egy|sḫm|t1=powerful, {{q|of the heart/mind}} daring, audacious|jb|t2=heart, mind|prj|alt3=pr.n|t3=has gone forth|mꜣꜥt|t4=Maat}}, thus ‘(the one) daring of heart (for whom) Maat has come forth’. However, {{m|egy||pr.n}} can also be interpreted as a participle and a preposition, {{m|egy|[[prj|pr]] [[n]]||going forth for}}, in which case the name would mean ‘(the one) daring of heart going forth for Maat’.

===Pronunciation===
{{egy-IPA-E}}

==Egyptian==

===Etymology===
{{af|egy|sḫm|t1=power, powerful|jrj|alt2=jr|t2=do, act|.f|pos3=third-person masculine singular suffix pronoun}}; the exact interpretation is not altogether clear. Taking {{m|egy|sḫm}} as a noun and {{m|egy||jr.f}} as a modifier, a meaning such as ‘acting power’ is sometimes suggested;<ref>As in Grandet, Pierre (2013) “The Ramesside State” in ''Ancient Egyptian Administration'', ed. Juan Carlos Moreno García, page 834</ref> this, however, fails to explain the suffix pronoun, which rather suggests an interpretation of {{m|egy||jr}} as a relative form instead of a participle, in which case the sense would be something like ‘the power that he makes’. Alternatively, some have taken {{m|egy|sḫm}} as a participle and {{m|egy||jr}} as a writing of the noun {{m|egy|jrw||visible form}} for an overall sense of ‘powerful of visible form’.<ref>As in Darnell, Colleen Manassa (2007) ''The Late Egyptian Underworld: Sarcophagi and Related Texts from the Nectanebid Period''</ref>

===Pronunciation===
{{egy-IPA-E}}

definitions: potentate, very powerful person or ruler, especially one of the feudal lords of the Middle Kingdom (dated: Pyramid Texts to 18th Dynasty)

==Egyptian==

===Etymology===
Unclear. Like many fifth-dynasty pharaohs’ birth names, this name may simply be a diminutive without any meaning of its own, perhaps of the pharaoh’s throne name {{m|egy|nfr-jr-kꜣ-rꜥ}} (in which case it may not be the actual name given at birth). Alternatively, some have tentatively attempted to explain it as {{af|egy|kꜣ|t1=life-force, sustenance|kꜣ|.j|t3=my}}, thus ‘my life-force is a life-force’.

{{egy-IPA-E}}

==Egyptian==

===Etymology===
Traditionally read and analyzed as {{af|egy|tꜣ|mrj}}, thus literally ‘beloved land’. However, in part due to the unusual writing of the latter word, alternative readings have recently been proposed, such as James P. Allen’s suggestion of {{af|egy|tꜣ|mr}}, literally ‘land of the hoe’, later revised to ‘canal-land’,<ref>{{R:egy:Allen|26|edition=3rd}}</ref> or Timofey Shmakov’s {{af|egy|tꜣ|m|rnpwt}}, literally ‘land in flowering’ (i.e. ‘Flowery/Blossomy Land’). In these cases, the {{m|egy||j}} in the word would not mark a separate consonant but rather a sound change of {{m|egy||r}} to {{m|egy||j}}, as is otherwise common in words such as {{m|egy|zwr}}.

===Pronunciation===

etymologies.etymology_text:
==Egyptian==

===Etymology===
{{compound|egy|twt|gloss1=image|ꜥnḫ|gloss2=living|jmn|gloss3=[[Amun]]|ḥqꜣ|gloss4=ruler|jwnw-šmꜥw|gloss5=Thebes|lit5=Heliopolis of Upper Egypt}}, thus literally meaning ‘The Living Image of [[Amun]], Ruler of the Heliopolis of Upper Egypt [i.e. [[Thebes]]]’. The compound is based on the pharaoh’s earlier name, {{m|egy|twt-ꜥnḫ-jtn|lit=living image of the [[Aten]]}}. A shorter form of {{m|egy||twt-ꜥnḫ-jmn-ḥqꜣ-jwnw-šmꜥw}} is found as {{m|egy|twt-ꜥnḫ-jmn||Tutankhamon}}.

* {{egy-IPA-E}}

Loprieno suggests an origin from {{af|egy|tj|wj|t1=while|pos2=first-person pronoun}}, with {{m|egy|tj}} from earlier {{m|egy|jsṯ|(j)sṯ}}, from Old Egyptian {{m|egy|jsk|(j)sk}}.<ref>{{R:egy:Loprieno}}</ref> Stauder argues against this hypothesis and instead proposes a development from {{af|egy|ntt|wj|pos1=complementizer|pos2=first-person pronoun}} with subsequent reanalysis.<ref>Stauder, Andréas (2016) “L’origine du pronom sujet néo-égyptien (''twꞽ'', ''twk'', ''sw'', etc.)” in ''Revue d’ Egyptologie'', volume 67, pages 141–155</ref> Regardless of origin, later reinterpreted as an element {{m|egy||tw}} + the suffix pronoun {{m|egy|.j}}.

===Pronunciation===
{{egy-IPA-E}}

==Egyptian==

===Etymology===
In origin from {{compound|egy|tj|n|gloss1=while|pos2=first-person plural dependent pronoun}}, with {{m|egy|tj}} from earlier {{m|egy|jsṯ|(j)sṯ}}, from Old Egyptian {{m|egy|jsk|(j)sk}}.<ref>{{R:egy:Loprieno}}</ref> Later reinterpreted as an element {{m|egy||tw}} + the suffix pronoun {{m|egy|.n}}.

===Pronunciation===
{{egy-IPA-E}}

==Egyptian==

===Etymology===
Loprieno suggests an origin from {{af|egy|tj|ṯw|t1=while|pos2=second-person masculine dependent pronoun}}, with {{m|egy|tj}} from earlier {{m|egy|jsṯ|(j)sṯ}}, from Old Egyptian {{m|egy|jsk|(j)sk}}.<ref>{{R:egy:Loprieno}}</ref> Stauder argues against this hypothesis and instead proposes a development from {{af|egy|ntt|.k|pos1=complementizer|pos2=second-person masculine suffix pronoun}} with subsequent reanalysis.<ref>Stauder, Andréas (2016) “L’origine du pronom sujet néo-égyptien (''twꞽ'', ''twk'', ''sw'', etc.)” in ''Revue d’ Egyptologie'', volume 67, pages 141–155</ref> Regardless of origin, later reinterpreted as an element {{m|egy||tw}} + the suffix pronoun {{m|egy|.k}}.

===Pronunciation===
{{egy-IPA-E}}

==Egyptian==

===Etymology===
Loprieno suggests an origin from {{af|egy|tj|ṯn|t1=while|pos2=second-person feminine dependent pronoun}}, with {{m|egy|tj}} from earlier {{m|egy|jsṯ|(j)sṯ}}, from Old Egyptian {{m|egy|jsk|(j)sk}}.<ref>{{R:egy:Loprieno}}</ref> Stauder argues against this hypothesis and instead proposes a development from {{af|egy|ntt|.ṯ|alt2=.t|pos1=complementizer|pos2=second-person feminine suffix pronoun}} with subsequent reanalysis.<ref>Stauder, Andréas (2016) “L’origine du pronom sujet néo-égyptien (''twꞽ'', ''twk'', ''sw'', etc.)” in ''Revue d’ Egyptologie'', volume 67, pages 141–155</ref> Regardless of origin, later reinterpreted as an element {{m|egy||tw}} + the suffix pronoun {{m|egy|.ṯ|.t}}.

===Pronunciation===
{{egy-IPA-E}}

==Egyptian==

===Etymology===
In origin from {{compound|egy|tj|tw|gloss1=while}} or {{m|egy|.tw|pos=impersonal pronoun}}, with {{m|egy|tj}} from earlier {{m|egy|jsṯ|(j)sṯ}}, from Old Egyptian {{m|egy|jsk|(j)sk}}.

===Pronunciation===
{{egy-IPA-E}}

definitions: used as the impersonal subject of any adverbial predicate; one, someone or something unspecified (dated: New Kingdom)

The reading of this word and related words (including the preposition below) has recently been contested. Werning and others have suggested that the traditional reading of  is wrong, with the New Kingdom reading more likely being dp, and the original reading conceivably either dp or ḏp. However, other Egyptologists argue for the traditional reading, and indeed the bulk of the current evidence seems to point to the traditional value.Werning, Daniel A. (2004) “The Sound Values of the Signs Gardiner D1 (Head) and T8 (Dagger)” in Lingua Aegyptia, volume 12, pages 183–204Peust, Carsten (2006) “Nochmals zur Lesung der Kopf-Hieroglyphe” in Göttinger Miszellen, volume 208, pages 7–8Schweitzer, Simon D. (2011) “Zum Lautwert einiger Hieroglyphen” in Zeitschrift für Agyptische Sprache und Altertumskunde, volume 138, pages 132–149Werning, Daniel A. (2015) Einführung in die hieroglyphisch-ägyptische Schrift und Sprache, pages 34–35:
“Die Einwände von (Schweitzer 2011) gegen die Lesung  sind nicht stichhaltig (was an anderer Stelle zu zeigen ist). Neben den unzweifelhaften Schreibungen von ‘Kopf’ als d:p im Amduat (Werning 2004: 196) ist noch folgender, kursivhieroglyphisch geschriebener Beleg hinzuzufügen: Dsr:r-Y1-d:p-tp:Z1-A40 ‘Der ein „sakrales“ Haupt hat’ (Papyrus BM 9971).”Roberson, Joshua Aaron (2018) “Tête-à-tête: Some Observations and Counter-Arguments Regarding a Contentious Phonological Value, dp or tp” in Lingua Aegyptia, volume 26, pages 185–202

definitions.usage_notes:
Some authors distinguish between the singular and plural as two different morphemes, treating plural  as a variant of Old Egyptian .wy or .wj and singular  as a variant of Old Egyptian .j; however, at least by Middle Egyptian, no distinction seems to have been made.

In Old Egyptian,  and its variants were used for the masculine plural, while .tj and its variants were used for the feminine plural. By Middle Egyptian,  had taken on both roles, making plural .tj rare.

This suffix is usually omitted entirely. When written at all, it is often written before the determinative of the verb.

==Egyptian== [[File:Relief plaque with a swallow MET DP243425.jpg|right|thumb]] ===Glyph origin=== Representing a swallow. ===Symbol=== {{head|egy|symbol|head=G36|tr=wr}} # {{ng|[[biliteral|Biliteral]] [[phonogram]] for {{m|egy||wr}}, including in the word {{m|egy|wr}}.}} ====Usage notes====
This glyph should not be confused with the similar G37 ({{m|egy|𓅪}}, a sparrow), a determinative for words related to the ideas of 'bad' or 'small'; note the difference in tail.

𓆨.references:
* {{R:egy:Gardiner|478}}
* Houlihan, Patrick F. (2002) “Animals in Egyptian art and hieroglyphics” in ''A history of the animal world in the ancient Near East'' (ed. Collins, Billie Jean), page 142

etymologies.etymology_text:
==Egyptian== ===Glyph origin===
Representing two reed [[panicle]]s, as a reduplication of i ({{m|egy|𓇋}}, phonogram for {{m|egy||j}}).
===Symbol=== {{head|egy|symbol|head=i-i|tr=y}} # {{ng|[[uniliteral|Uniliteral]] [[phonogram]] for {{m|egy||y}}.}} ====Usage notes==== Some [[Appendix:Egyptian transliteration schemes|transliteration schemes]] treat this as a simple variant of its unreduplicated counterpart, transliterating them all alike as {{m|egy||j}}. ===References=== * {{R:egy:Gardiner|481}} [[Category:Green Egyptian hieroglyphs]] [[Category:Blue Egyptian hieroglyphs]]

==Egyptian== ===Glyph origin===
A form of {{egy-h|N37}} ({{m|egy|𓈙}}, representing a pool) with a few diagonal lines across the interior to suggest ripples of water and distinguish it from similar glyphs; this form originated in hieratic and appeared occasionally in semi-cursive hieroglyphs during the Old Kingdom (and later); it rarely appeared in hieroglyphs proper before the Late Period.
===Symbol=== {{head|egy|symbol|head={{egy-h|N37A}}|tr=š}} # {{altform|egy|𓈙}} ===References=== * Henry George Fischer, ''Ancient Egyptian Calligraphy: A Beginner's Guide'' (1988), page 13

𓈚.references: * Henry George Fischer, ''Ancient Egyptian Calligraphy: A Beginner's Guide'' (1988), page 13

etymologies.etymology_text:
==Egyptian== ===Glyph origin===
An occasional variant form of {{egy-h|N37}} ({{m|egy|𓈙}}).
===Symbol=== {{head|egy|symbol|head={{egy-h|N38}}|tr=š}} # {{altform|egy|𓈙}} ===Further reading=== * Richey L. Waugh, ''The Eye and Man in Ancient Egypt'' (2018), page 212 (says this sign is found at least as early as the Pyramid Texts of Unas)

==Egyptian== ===Glyph origin===
A detailed Old Kingdom form of {{egy-h|N37}} ({{m|egy|𓈙}}, representing a pool) with its interior covered in vertical zigzags of rippling water.
===Symbol=== {{head|egy|symbol|head={{egy-h|N39}}|tr=š}} # {{altform|egy|𓈙}} ===References=== * Henry George Fischer, ''Ancient Egyptian Calligraphy: A Beginner's Guide'' (1988), page 13

𓈜.references: * Henry George Fischer, ''Ancient Egyptian Calligraphy: A Beginner's Guide'' (1988), page 13

==Egyptian==
{{wikipedia|Ankh}}

===Glyph origin===
Disputed. Traditionally it was interpreted as a sandal strap, but this explanation is now increasingly rejected. Fischer describes it as originally representing an elaborate amuletic bow, noting that the lower part represents the two ends of the cord next to each other; the form of the glyph in the Archaic Period generally showed these two ends widely separated instead of together as in the later ankh. Westendorf hypothesizes that it originally represented a sort of belt similar to the [[w:knot of Isis|knot of Isis]].

==Egyptian==

===Glyph origin===
A depiction of a knife with a curved handle. In an example from Rekhmire's tomb, it is colored red, either to represent danger or copper. 

Compare the Chinese character {{m|mul|刀|sc=Hani}} (Bronze inscriptional form [[File:刀-bronze-shang.svg|25px]]).

===Symbol===
{{head|egy|symbol|head=<hiero>T30</hiero>}}

# {{ng|Ideogram for cutting, used in {{m|egy|šꜥ}}, as well as {{m|egy|jw}}, {{m|egy|smꜣ}}, {{m|egy|zfṯ}}, {{m|egy|zft}}, etc.}}

==Egyptian== ===Glyph origin===
This sign does not actually exist in hieroglyphic text; it is an artificial glyph used for transcribing a hieratic character deriving from the convergence of the hieratic forms of {{egy-h|Sn:n}} and {{egy-h|sn}}. Compare the further simplified Demotic form of the character, {{t2i-Egyd|sn-2}} or {{t2i-Egyd|sn}}.
===Symbol=== {{head|egy|symbol|head={{egy-h|V49A}}|tr=-}} # {{ng|Used in transcribing [[hieratic]] [[sign]]s into [[hieroglyph]]s in cases where it is not clear whether a given hieratic sign represents {{egy-h|Sn:n}} ({{m|egy||šn}}) or {{egy-h|sn}} ({{m|egy||sn}}). See {{m|egy|𓍲}} or {{m|egy|𓌢}} for usage.}} ===References=== * Černý, Jaroslav; Israelit-Groll, Sarah; Eyre, Christopher (1993) ''A Late Egyptian Grammar'', fourth edition, pages 3–4

𓍴.references: * Černý, Jaroslav; Israelit-Groll, Sarah; Eyre, Christopher (1993) ''A Late Egyptian Grammar'', fourth edition, pages 3–4

etymologies.etymology_text:
==Egyptian== ===Glyph origin===
Generally taken to represent a conical loaf of bread, this glyph was conventionally outlined in black or blue, often with white fill and a red inner triangle; compare [[𓏏]] X1. Nunn writes that the interpretation of this glyph as bread is questionable: "neither X1 nor X8 is represented as bread on offering tables in funerary scenes"; in e.g. [[𓏐]] X2 and [[𓏑]] X3 bread is yellow; and conical bread molds did exist but were rounded: this glyph's shape is more like an angular "funerary cone", but those were white or red.
===Symbol=== {{head|egy|symbol|head=X8|tr=(r)ḏj}} # {{ng|[[ideogram|Ideogram]] for {{m|egy|rḏj|rḏj, ḏj|give}}.}} ===References=== * David Nunn, [https://www.phrp.be/Palaeography.php A Palaeography of Polychrome Hieroglyphs] (2020) [[Category:Polychrome Egyptian hieroglyphs]]

𓏙.references:
* David Nunn, [https://www.phrp.be/Palaeography.php A Palaeography of Polychrome Hieroglyphs] (2020)

etymologies.etymology_text:
==Egyptian== ===Glyph origin===
A readaptation into hieroglyphs of the abbreviated [[hieratic]] form of {{m|egy|𓅱}} (w). The hieratic form grows increasingly common from the 9th dynasty onward, whereas its hieroglyphic readaptation first becomes notably common during the reign of {{w|Akhenaten}}.
===Symbol=== {{head|egy|symbol|head=W|tr=w}} # {{alt form|egy|𓅱}} (w) ====Usage notes====
This glyph should not be confused with the extremely similar V1 ({{m|egy|𓍢}}), which serves as a phonogram for {{m|egy||šn}}, a determinative for rope, and a numeral for 100.
====Descendants==== * {{desctree|phn|𐤅}} ===References=== * {{R:egy:Gardiner|537}}

==Egyptian==
[[File:Edfu 15 cartouche hieroglyphs decolorized.jpg|right|thumb|A cartouche of {{w|Ptolemy VI Philometor|Ptolemy VI}} at Edfu, using this hieroglyph.]]

Representing a platform or [[plinth]].

===Symbol===
{{head|egy|symbol|head=<hiero>mAa</hiero>|tr=mꜣꜥ}}

# {{ng|[[triliteral|Triliteral]] for {{m|egy||mꜣꜥ}}, e.g. for the word {{m|egy|mꜣꜥ}} in {{m|egy|mꜣꜥ-ḫrw}}.}}
